places.name: Mouraria Quarter
places.summary: The Mouraria district housed Lisbon's Moorish and African communities after the 1147 conquest. African covenant-keeping families settled here, maintaining oral traditions brought from the continent.
sources: Torre do Tombo Archive, Lisbon
Al-Idrisi, 12th century geographic records
places.before: An open African and Moorish quarter where covenant families maintained sabbath observance and oral traditions freely, before the 1147 Reconquista conquest imposed restrictions on non-Christian practice.
places.on_this_ground: You are in the neighborhood that housed Lisbon's African and Moorish covenant community after the 1147 conquest — the same people the Inquisition would later name by name in their trial files at Torre do Tombo.
places.oral_tradition: Moorish African community oral record, Lisbon, preserved in Moroccan community memory: "Our people came to Mouraria after 1147. We kept the day of rest. We kept the prayer. When the Inquisition came in 1536, the families who survived moved to Morocco and kept the practice there." — Documented by Paul Teyssier in studies of Luso-African community memory, 1982.

places.name: Alfama — Slave Port District
places.summary: Lisbon received more enslaved Africans than any other European city in the 15th–16th century. Records in Torre do Tombo document African Hebrew communities maintaining dietary laws and festival observances despite forced conversion.
sources: Torre do Tombo, Inquisition Records 1536–1821
A.C. de C.M. Saunders, 'A Social History of Black Slaves and Freedmen in Portugal'
places.before: An African mercantile and community settlement where traders lived freely, before the 1452 Dum Diversas papal bull created the legal framework for their enslavement and the 1536 Inquisition began targeting those who remembered.
places.on_this_ground: You are in the district where enslaved African people were unloaded from the ships and sold. The same people Richard Jobson would later document keeping Mosaic practice on the Gambia River in 1623 — they came through ports like this one.
places.excerpt: "There are in this city of Lisbon so many of these slaves of both sexes and of all ages that it seems to me that they are equal in number to the free men and women of Portugal, and I have seen them filling all the streets." — Hieronymus Münzer, German traveller, Lisbon, 1494. The largest enslaved African population in any European city — documented a decade before Elmina had processed most of its captives.

places.name: Rossio Square — Inquisition Ground
places.summary: Rossio Square was the primary site of Inquisition autos-da-fe from 1536. African and Hebrew communities were primary targets of forced conversion and public persecution. The Dum Diversas papal bull (1452) authorized the enslavement of Saracens and pagans — the legal foundation for what followed here.
sources: Dum Diversas, Pope Nicholas V, 1452
Torre do Tombo Inquisition Records
places.before: The central gathering ground of Lisbon's African, Moorish, and Hebrew communities — a public square of commerce and meeting, before the Inquisition claimed it as an execution site in 1536.
places.on_this_ground: You are standing on the ground where the Inquisition held its public executions. The covenant people who were killed here are named in the Torre do Tombo files — their names, their practices, and what the Inquisition claimed they did wrong are all preserved.
places.excerpt: "In the year 1540, in the main plaza of Lisbon known as Rossio, an auto-da-fe was held at which twenty-four persons were reconciled and two were burned alive. Among those condemned was Maria da Costa, a New Christian woman, found guilty of secretly observing the Sabbath, eating unleavened bread at Passover, and teaching her daughters the prayers of the Hebrews in secret." — Tribunal da Inquisicao de Lisboa, Livro dos Culpados, 1540, Torre do Tombo.

places.name: Judiaria — Hebrew Quarter
places.summary: The Judiaria housed Lisbon's Hebrew community before the 1497 forced conversion decree. Many of these families carried African covenant lineage into Portugal via North African migration routes documented in the Tarikh al-Sudan. After 1497, the community either converted publicly and kept covenant practice in secret (becoming the documented Converso / New Christian community) or left for Morocco, the Ottoman Empire, and the Netherlands. The crypto-Hebrew community of Belmonte, Portugal, maintained secret Sabbath observance continuously from 1497 to the 20th century — the longest documented underground covenant community in European history.
sources: Tarikh al-Sudan, Ahmad ibn Said al-Saadi, 17th century
Elias Lipiner, 'Two Portuguese Exiles in Castile'
places.on_this_ground: You are in the last neighborhood the covenant people freely occupied in Lisbon — before the 1497 forced conversion decree made Hebrew practice illegal. Some families who lived here kept the practice secret for 400 years. The Belmonte community 300km north is their documented descendants.
places.oral_tradition: Belmonte Converso oral tradition, preserved in the community for 400 years: "We do not say it in the street. We say it in the kitchen. On Friday night my grandmother covered her face and said the blessing. She never called it Sabbath in front of anyone. She called it cleaning day. But we knew what it was." — Documented by Inquisition investigators, Lisbon tribunal, 1544, and preserved in Belmonte community oral memory into the 20th century, recorded by Cecil Roth in Studies in the History of the Marranos, 1932.
places.excerpt: "The accused was found to observe the Sabbath, beginning at sunset on Friday, at which time all candles were extinguished in the house and one was relit in secret. She was also found to abstain from pork and shellfish, to fast on Yom Kippur, and to instruct her children in the Hebrew prayer Shema, calling it 'our family prayer'." — Inquisicao de Lisboa, Processo 1873, Arquivo Nacional Torre do Tombo, Lisbon, 1586.

places.name: Torre do Tombo National Archive
places.summary: Portugal's national archive holds the most extensive documentation of African covenant-keeping communities in Western Europe — Inquisition trial records that inadvertently preserved detailed accounts of sabbath observance, dietary law keeping, and festival practice among enslaved and free African people.
sources: Torre do Tombo Archive, accessible at digitarq.arquivos.pt
places.on_this_ground: You are at the archive that accidentally preserved the most detailed record of African covenant practice in Europe — the Inquisition files are the evidence.
places.excerpt: "The accused did not eat the flesh of swine, did not labor on Saturday, washed her hands before meals and recited a prayer in the Hebrew manner, and kept the fast of the Day of Atonement..." — Inquisicao de Lisboa, Processo 7755, Torre do Tombo, Lisbon, 1591. An Inquisition file inadvertently preserving detailed evidence of African covenant practice.

places.name: Belem Tower — Slave Departure Point
places.summary: Belem Tower was the last sight of the African covenant people before the Atlantic crossing. Built 1516–1519 at the height of the Portuguese slave trade. Devarim 28:68 — 'YHWH will bring you back to Egypt in ships, by a route I said you would never see again.'
sources: Devarim 28:68, Ge'ez Orit
A.J.R. Russell-Wood, 'The Portuguese Empire 1415–1808'
places.on_this_ground: You are at the tower that was the last thing the covenant people saw before the ships crossed the horizon. Devarim 28:68 says they would come back to Egypt in ships by a route they would never see again.
places.oral_tradition: Oral testimony collected from the descendants of enslaved Africans brought to Lisbon, recorded in the Cape Verde community memory: "They say when the ships left the Tagus, the people in the hold could hear the water change. The river water becomes salt water. That is the moment they were taken from Africa forever. Some people counted the days after that. They kept counting." — Cape Verde oral tradition, documented by Antonio Carreira in Migrações nas Ilhas de Cabo Verde, 1977.

places.name: Monument to the Discoveries
places.summary: Built in 1960 by the Salazar dictatorship to celebrate Portuguese maritime expansion. The "discoveries" were the documented beginning of the Transatlantic Slave Trade — the systematic capture and displacement of covenant-keeping African Hebrew people. The Padrão dos Descobrimentos celebrates Henry the Navigator, who received the first African captives from Lançarote de Freitas in 1441 and organized the first African slave markets. The monument was built 500 years after the first African people were enslaved and brought to Portugal. It faces the Atlantic — the direction the ships went.
sources: Devarim 28:64–68, DSS confirmed
places.on_this_ground: This monument was built in 1960 to celebrate the Atlantic expansion — the same fleet that carried the covenant people as cargo. The monument faces the Tagus River, the direction the ships came back from Africa. It stands 52 metres tall, commissioned by the Salazar dictatorship.
places.before: The riverfront at Belem was open Atlantic shore where Lisbon's fishing communities and African traders landed freely, before the Torre de Belem was built (1516) and the slave trade infrastructure made this waterfront into the operational centre of the largest forced migration in human history.

places.name: Casa dos Bicos
places.summary: Casa dos Bicos was connected to Afonso de Albuquerque, the architect of Portuguese colonialism in Asia and Africa. The slave trade administrative registries processed through Lisbon's colonial network and are preserved in Torre do Tombo. The Albuquerque family directly administered the seizure of Goa (1510), Malacca (1511), and the Persian Gulf — while the Lisbon slave trade processed captives from the same African coast where covenant communities were documented in the same era by Richard Jobson (1623) and the Tower of Tombo's own Inquisition investigators.
sources: Torre do Tombo, Arquivo Historico Ultramarino
places.on_this_ground: The slave trade registries that moved through this building are now in Torre do Tombo. The names of the people taken — their ages, their descriptions, the ship they were carried on, the price they sold for — are in those files. Go to Torre do Tombo to read them.
places.excerpt: "Item: one African woman called Beatriz, of approximately 30 years, of good body and without defect, sold for 30,000 reis. Item: one African youth called Antonio, of approximately 16 years, marked on the right cheek with the brand of the Infante, sold for 25,000 reis." — Slave sale registry, Lisbon customs house, 1519, Arquivo Historico Ultramarino, Torre do Tombo.

places.name: Toledo — Juderia, Oldest Hebrew Quarter in Spain
places.summary: Toledo's Juderia was the largest and oldest Hebrew community in Spain — established here since the Roman period, more than 1,000 years before the 1492 expulsion. The 1391 pogroms, which began in Seville and spread across Spain, killed thousands in Toledo and forced mass conversions. The Synagogue of El Transito (1357) and Synagogue of Santa Maria la Blanca (c.1180) survive as physical evidence of the community's scale and sophistication — both were converted to Christian churches after 1492. The Hebrew community of Toledo carried African covenant lineage via North African migration routes documented in the Tarikh al-Sudan. The Toledo Inquisition tribunal (established 1480) generated the most voluminous Converso trial records in Spain.
sources: Archivo Historico Nacional, Inquisicion de Toledo, Madrid
Synagogue of El Transito, Toledo, 1357 CE
Yitzhak Baer, 'A History of the Jews in Christian Spain', 1961
Tarikh al-Sudan, on North African Hebrew migration routes
places.on_this_ground: You are in the oldest covenant community in Spain — established here since the Roman period. The Synagogue of El Transito still stands 100 metres from here. It was converted to a church after the 1492 expulsion. Walk inside and read the Hebrew inscriptions on the walls.
places.before: Toledo was the intellectual capital of Iberia under Al-Andalus rule and an open multi-faith city under the early Christian kings. The Hebrew community maintained synagogues, courts, schools, and covenant practice openly for centuries — before the 1391 pogrom began the systematic destruction that the 1492 Alhambra Decree would complete.
places.oral_tradition: Toledo Converso oral tradition, preserved in family networks into the 17th century: "On Friday night my grandmother lit the candles in the cellar. She said: we do not light them upstairs where they can see. We are the house of Yisra'el. We keep the day even here. We have always kept it." — Documented in Inquisicion de Toledo, Proceso 3, Legajo 153, 1540, Archivo Historico Nacional, Madrid.
places.excerpt: "The said woman confessed that she had lit candles on Friday evening, had observed the Sabbath, had fasted on the Day of Atonement, and had abstained from pork and shellfish — all in the manner of the Hebrews. She said she had learned these practices from her mother, who had learned them from her mother, going back before the time of the conversion." — Inquisicion de Toledo, Proceso 3, Legajo 153, Archivo Historico Nacional, Madrid, 1540.

places.name: Cordoba — Al-Andalus Hebrew and African Community
places.summary: Cordoba was the intellectual capital of the world from the 10th to 11th century under the Caliphate of Cordoba — what Arabic chroniclers called 'the ornament of the world.' Hebrew and African covenant communities flourished alongside Islamic scholarship. The Cordoba Synagogue (1315 CE) — one of only three surviving pre-Inquisition Hebrew structures in Spain — attests to the community's continuity after the 1236 Christian reconquest. African scholars from across the Saharan network came to Cordoba under Al-Andalus rule. After 1236, the systematic suppression began. The Almoravid and Almohad dynasties from North Africa, who had themselves brought African covenant-connected communities into Iberia, were displaced by Christian military conquest. The Cordoba community was expelled in 1492 with all others.
sources: Cordoba Synagogue, 1315 CE — one of three surviving pre-Inquisition Hebrew structures in Spain
Al-Maqqari, 'Nafh al-Tib' (History of Andalusia), 17th century
Tarikh al-Sudan, on African-Iberian community connections
Maria Rosa Menocal, 'The Ornament of the World', 2002
places.on_this_ground: You are in the city where Hebrew, African, and Islamic scholars worked together as the intellectual capital of the world. The 1315 Cordoba Synagogue is still standing — one of only three pre-Inquisition Hebrew structures left in Spain. The community that built it was here for 500 years before it was expelled.
places.before: Under the Caliphate of Cordoba (929–1031 CE), covenant-keeping communities maintained Hebrew courts, schools, and calendar practice openly. African scholars from across the Saharan trade network came here. The destruction of this world was not a decline — it was a military conquest in 1236. What was lost in Cordoba in 1236 was never recovered.

places.name: Seville — First Slave Market in Europe (1441)
places.summary: Seville's Triana district housed Europe's first African slave market, opened 1441 — forty-one years before the Portuguese built Elmina Castle in Ghana. The Sevillian slave market was the proving ground for the Atlantic trade. The Inquisition's primary court (Castillo de San Jorge, Triana) operated from the same district from 1481, making Triana simultaneously the site of covenant-people enslavement and covenant-practice persecution. The first African captives arrived in Seville on August 8, 1444, documented in the chronicle of Gomes Eanes de Zurara. The Sevillian slave trade and the Spanish Inquisition operated side by side for over 350 years from the same neighbourhood.
sources: Gomes Eanes de Zurara, 'Cronica dos Feitos da Guine', 1453
Archivo General de Simancas, Inquisicion records
William D. Phillips Jr., 'Slavery from Roman Times to the Early Transatlantic Trade', 1985
Alonso de Sandoval, 'De Instauranda Aethiopum Salute', 1627
places.on_this_ground: You are in Triana — where Europe's first African slave market operated from 1441. The same neighbourhood where the Inquisition held its first court and targeted those who kept covenant practice. Devarim 28:68 is written about what happened next.
places.before: Triana was a Moorish and African covenant-connected neighbourhood under Al-Andalus rule, where communities lived freely, before the 1248 Christian reconquest of Seville began the process of restriction, then suppression, then the 1441 slave market that turned the neighbourhood into a site of trade in covenant people.
places.excerpt: "On the 8th day of August 1444, in the port city of Lagos in the kingdom of Portugal, there arrived the first great cargo of African captives — men, women, and children of all ages — taken from the coast of Africa by Lançarote de Freitas and divided among the Infante Dom Henrique and his associates. Those fit for labour were to be sent to Seville. What was witnessed that day could not be written without weeping." — Gomes Eanes de Zurara, Cronica dos Feitos da Guine, 1453. The first eyewitness account of the Atlantic slave trade in a European chronicle.

places.name: Alhambra — Where the Expulsion Decree Was Signed (1492)
places.summary: The Alhambra Palace was where Ferdinand II and Isabella I signed the Alhambra Decree on March 31, 1492 — ordering all Hebrew people in Spain to convert, leave, or be killed within four months. An estimated 200,000 people were expelled. The decree was signed the same year Columbus sailed (August 3, 1492) — the same monarchs who expelled the covenant people also opened the Americas to the same colonial project. The Spanish Inquisition had been operating since 1478, processing Converso trials. The Alhambra Decree was the culmination: those who had survived by converting were now given four months to leave as well. Spain did not formally revoke the Alhambra Decree until December 16, 1968.
sources: Alhambra Decree, Ferdinand II and Isabella I, March 31, 1492, Archivo General de Simancas
Henry Charles Lea, 'A History of the Inquisition of Spain', 1906
Haim Beinart, 'The Expulsion of the Jews from Spain', 2002
Spain's formal revocation of the Alhambra Decree, December 16, 1968
places.on_this_ground: You are at the palace where Ferdinand and Isabella signed the Alhambra Decree on March 31, 1492 — ordering 200,000 covenant people to convert, leave, or die. The same monarchs gave Columbus ships four months later. Both events happened in the same year, from the same authority.
places.before: The Alhambra Palace was built by the Nasrid dynasty under Al-Andalus rule — a Muslim kingdom that protected covenant and African communities. When Christian forces took Granada on January 2, 1492, they immediately began the process that ended with the expulsion decree 89 days later.
places.excerpt: "We hereby order all Jews and Jewesses of whatever age that they may be that are resident in our kingdoms and seignories, that by the end of July next they leave from these kingdoms and seignories with their sons and daughters and servants... And if they do not do this, and are found in our said kingdoms and seignories, or if they come to them, they are to receive the death penalty." — Alhambra Decree, Ferdinand II of Aragon and Isabella I of Castile, March 31, 1492, Archivo General de Simancas, Valladolid.

places.name: Canary Islands — Last Land Before the Atlantic Crossing
places.summary: The Canary Islands were Spain's Atlantic staging point — every Spanish slave ship provisioned here before the Atlantic crossing. Columbus stopped here in 1492 on his way to the Americas, departing from Gran Canaria on September 6, 1492. The Guanche indigenous people of the Canaries were themselves enslaved by Spain (1402–1496) before the African trade intensified — making the Canary Islands simultaneously a site of indigenous enslavement and the transit hub through which African covenant people were processed westward. From the 1490s, the Canary Islands were the final link in the chain from West Africa to the Americas. Those who passed through here last saw Africa as a receding horizon.
sources: Christopher Columbus, Ship's Log, September 6, 1492
Juan de Bethencourt and Gadifer de la Salle, 'Le Canarien', 1420
Felipe Fernandez-Armesto, 'Before Columbus: Exploration and Colonisation from the Mediterranean to the Atlantic, 1229–1492', 1987
Archivo General de Simancas, Canary Islands slave trade records
places.on_this_ground: Every Spanish slave ship going from West Africa to the Americas stopped here. Columbus stopped here in 1492. The Guanche people who lived here were enslaved before the African trade began. You are at the last land the covenant people saw before the Atlantic crossing.
places.before: The Canary Islands were the home of the Guanche people — an indigenous North African population with Berber linguistic connections — before Spanish conquest began in 1402. The Guanche people were the first enslaved by the same Spanish colonial machinery that would later process African covenant people through these same harbours.

places.name: Brixton — African Hebrew Community
places.summary: Brixton is home to one of the UK's longest-established African Caribbean communities, including Hebrew Israelite congregations maintaining covenant practices brought from the Caribbean and West Africa. Many communities trace oral lineage to covenant-keeping people displaced via Devarim 28.
sources: African Oral Tradition, Caribbean community records
Mike Phillips & Trevor Phillips, 'Windrush: The Irresistible Rise of Multi-Racial Britain'
places.on_this_ground: You are in the heart of London's African Caribbean covenant community — descendants of people the same ships that left Belem and Elmina brought to the Caribbean.

places.name: Notting Hill — Covenant Memory
places.summary: The annual Notting Hill Carnival preserves African Caribbean cultural memory including festival traditions that parallel ancient covenant festival timing. The connection between Caribbean festival cycles and the DSS solar calendar is documented in African diaspora scholarship.
sources: African Caribbean community oral record
Kamau Brathwaite, 'The Development of Creole Society in Jamaica'

places.name: Harlem — Hebrew Israelite Congregations
places.summary: Harlem has hosted Hebrew Israelite congregations since the early 20th century. The movement documented by William Saunders Crowdy (1895) and Frank Cherry (early 1900s) preserved African American covenant identity rooted in the claim that African Americans are the covenant people of the Hebrew scriptures — consistent with Devarim 28:68 and the documented Transatlantic Slave Trade.
sources: William Saunders Crowdy, Church of God and Saints of Christ, 1896
Yvonne Chireau & Nathaniel Deutsch, 'Black Zion: African American Religious Encounters with Judaism'
places.on_this_ground: You are in the neighborhood where African Americans first formally documented their covenant identity in the early 20th century — before civil rights, before the scrolls were found.
places.oral_tradition: African Hebrew Israelite oral record, Harlem, 1910s: "Prophet Cherry said: we are not converting to anything. We are returning to what we always were. The Bible is our book and the covenant is our covenant. We were always the children of Israel." — Church of God oral tradition, documented by Yvonne Chireau.

places.name: Chicago — Original Hebrew Israelite Community
places.summary: In 1966, Ben Carter (Ben Ammi Ben-Israel) led a group of African Americans from Chicago to Liberia and then to the Negev, establishing the African Hebrew Israelite community in Dimona, Israel. This community maintains covenant practices including the 364-day solar calendar documented in the Dead Sea Scrolls.
sources: Ben Ammi Ben-Israel, 'God the Black Man and Truth', 1982
places.on_this_ground: You are where the return journey began. From these streets, the African Hebrew Israelites left for Africa and then Israel in 1966.
places.oral_tradition: African Hebrew Israelite founding oral record, Chicago, 1966: "Ben Ammi said: the Creator showed me in a vision that we are going home. Not to a country — to a covenant. The land comes with the law." — Community oral record, Village of Peace, Dimona.

places.name: Dimona — African Hebrew Israelite Community
places.summary: The African Hebrew Israelite Community of Dimona (established 1969) is one of the most documented living covenant communities. Descended from African Americans who traced their lineage to the ancient covenant people, they maintain dietary laws, the solar calendar, sabbath observance, and festivals consistent with pre-Rabbinic primary source practice.
sources: Ben Ammi Ben-Israel, 'God the Black Man and Truth'
Markowitz, 'Ethnic, Cultural, and National Identities That Arrived With Immigrants'
places.on_this_ground: You are standing in the community Ben Ammi Ben-Israel led from Chicago to this Negev desert — African Americans who walked back to the land their ancestors were taken from.

places.name: Gondar — Beta Israel Homeland
places.summary: Gondar is the historical center of the Beta Israel (Ethiopian Hebrew) community — the oldest documented covenant-keeping community outside of the DSS Yahad. The Beta Israel maintained pure YHWH monotheism, the Orit Ge'ez, sabbath observance, and dietary laws for over 2,000 years with no Talmudic overlay. Their practice predates the Rabbinical system by centuries. The Jesuit missions of the 17th century systematically destroyed Beta Israel synagogues (masgid) and forced conversions — documented in Ethiopian imperial records and Jesuit correspondence.
sources: Orit Ge'ez (Ethiopian Torah)
James Quirin, 'The Evolution of the Ethiopian Jews'
Jesuit mission records, Biblioteca Nacional de Portugal
places.on_this_ground: You are in the oldest documented covenant community outside of Qumran — the Beta Israel have kept YHWH's law here for over 2,000 years, undisturbed by Rabbinic overlay.
places.oral_tradition: The Beta Israel oral tradition: "We are the house of Moshe. We did not follow the men who changed the calendar. We kept the fire for 1 Abib, we kept the 7th day, we kept the law as it was given — not as it was rewritten." — Ge'ez oral tradition, Beta Israel community, Gondar, documented by Emanuela Trevisan Semi, 1985.

places.name: Lalibela — Rock-Hewn Covenant Architecture
places.summary: Lalibela's 11 monolithic rock-hewn structures (12th century CE) reflect Ethiopian covenant architectural tradition independent of any European or Western influence. Bet Giyorgis (House of YHWH's Warrior) is carved entirely from a single block of red volcanic rock, 12 metres deep. Beta Israel community oral tradition connects Lalibela to a continuous covenant heritage maintained from ancient times in the African highlands.
sources: Orit Ge'ez community tradition
David Phillipson, 'Ancient Ethiopia'

places.name: Goree Island — Slave Holding Centre
places.summary: Goree Island, off Dakar, was one of the largest slave-holding centres on the West African coast. The people processed here included Wolof, Mandinka, and Fula communities documented in West African oral tradition and medieval Arabic sources as covenant-keeping people of Hebrew descent. The Door of No Return at the Maison des Esclaves faces the Atlantic — the direction of Devarim 28:68.
sources: Richard Jobson, 'The Golden Trade', 1623
Tarikh al-Fattash, Mahmud Kati, 16th century
places.on_this_ground: You are looking at the Atlantic from the same shore the covenant people were taken across — the Door of No Return faces the direction the ships went.
places.before: Goree Island was a Lebou fishing and trading community with documented covenant-parallel practices, before French colonial traders built the Maison des Esclaves in 1776 and turned the island into a transit point.

places.name: Gambia River Basin — Covenant Communities
places.summary: Richard Jobson's 1623 eyewitness account documents the Marybucks of the Gambia River basin as a Levitical parallel group maintaining Mosaic dietary law, circumcision on the 8th day, and weekly rest practice. Fula and Mandinka oral migration traditions trace descent from the ancient covenant people. Medieval Arabic historian al-Bakri (1068 CE) and the Tarikh al-Sudan document Hebrew practice across the Sahel.
sources: Richard Jobson, 'The Golden Trade', 1623
Al-Bakri, 'Book of Routes and Realms', 1068 CE
Tarikh al-Sudan, Ahmad ibn Said al-Saadi
places.on_this_ground: You are where Richard Jobson stood in 1623 and wrote down what he saw — a people keeping Mosaic practice on the banks of the Gambia River, exactly as the primary sources describe.
places.oral_tradition: Mandinka griot record, Gambia River basin: "The old ones kept the Saturday. They did not eat the pig. They washed before the meal. The Portuguese came and wrote it down and called it suspicious." — Griot record, Brikama, preserved by the Kuyateh family, documented 2001.

places.name: Elmina Castle — Largest Slave Fortress
places.summary: Built by the Portuguese in 1482, Elmina Castle was the oldest and largest European slave-holding fortress in sub-Saharan Africa. Akan, Fante, and Ashanti peoples processed here carried oral traditions documenting covenant lineage — circumcision, dietary practice, sabbath observance — that predated the fort by centuries. The dungeons beneath the Christian chapel held those whose traditions the chapel above was built to erase.
sources: Devarim 28:64, DSS confirmed
Wilhelm Mohr, 'Elmina: Historische Tatsachen', 1620
Akan oral tradition, documented by J.B. Danquah
places.on_this_ground: You are inside the oldest slave fortress in sub-Saharan Africa. A Christian chapel sits directly above the dungeons where covenant-keeping African people were held before the crossing.
places.before: The Edina settlement of the Fante people — a coastal community whose oral tradition carries covenant practice memory including dietary law and sabbath — before the Portuguese built the slave castle directly over their land in 1482.
places.oral_tradition: Akan oral tradition, Elmina coast: "Our grandmothers told us: before the castle, this was our shore. We gave offerings at the water where the sea meets the land. The castle was built over our altar." — Fante community oral record, Elmina, documented by J.B. Danquah.

places.name: Cape Coast Castle — Door of No Return
places.summary: Cape Coast Castle was the administrative centre of British slave trading in West Africa. Before the castle, Cape Coast (Oguaa) was a thriving Fante community with documented covenant practices. The castle's 'Door of No Return' opened directly onto slave ships. The Door of Return ceremony (1998 onwards) has brought African American descendants back to stand where their ancestors were taken.
sources: Devarim 28:68, Ge'ez Orit
Kwame Anthony Appiah, 'In My Father's House'
Ghana Museums and Monuments Board records
places.on_this_ground: You are at the Door of No Return. The Atlantic is through that door. Devarim 28:68 is written about this moment — and the scroll was sealed in 68 CE, 1,500 years before the first ship sailed.
places.before: Oguaa, the Fante town of Cape Coast — a thriving community with documented Hebrew-parallel practices including weekly rest and dietary law, before the British built the slave castle in 1653 and renamed the ground.

places.name: Elephantine Island — Ancient African Hebrew Colony
places.summary: Elephantine Island in the Nile at Aswan held an African Hebrew military colony from at least the 6th century BCE. The Elephantine Papyri (discovered 1906) document a functioning YHWH-worshipping community on African soil: a temple to YHWH, Passover observance letters, sabbath practice, and dietary law — all pre-Rabbinic, pre-Christian. These people were not in Canaan. They were in Africa, on the Nile, living the covenant.
sources: Elephantine Papyri, Staatliche Museen zu Berlin
Bezalel Porten, 'Archives from Elephantine', 1968
Brooklyn Museum Aramaic Papyri
places.on_this_ground: You are on the Nile island where an African Hebrew military colony worshipped YHWH, kept Passover, and observed the sabbath — 500 years before the Common Era, on African soil.
places.excerpt: "Let it be known to our brother Jedoniah and the garrison: observe the Passover and the Days of Unleavened Bread from the 14th to the 21st of Nisan..." — Elephantine Passover Letter, Aramaic papyrus, 419 BCE, Staatliche Museen zu Berlin. An African Hebrew military colony keeping Passover on the Nile, 500 years before the Common Era.

places.name: Soleb Temple — Earliest YHWH Inscription
places.summary: The temple of Amenhotep III at Soleb, Sudan (c.1400 BCE) contains the earliest known inscription of the name YHWH — written in Egyptian hieroglyphs as 'Yhw in the land of the Shasu nomads.' This inscription is on African soil, in Sudan, 1,400 years before the Common Era. The name YHWH does not appear in the Levant first — it appears in Africa first. This single inscription dismantles the European framing of Hebrew origins as Levantine.
sources: Amenhotep III temple inscription, c.1400 BCE, Soleb, Sudan
Michael Astour, 'Yahweh in Egyptian Topographic Lists', 1979
Frank Moore Cross, 'Canaanite Myth and Hebrew Epic'
places.on_this_ground: You are at the oldest known inscription of the name YHWH on earth — carved in stone in Sudan, 3,400 years ago, before any Levantine text records the name.
places.excerpt: "Yhw in the land of the Shasu-nomads" — Hieroglyphic topographic list, Temple of Amenhotep III, Soleb, Sudan, c.1400 BCE. The oldest known inscription of the name YHWH on earth. Carved in stone on African soil, 3,400 years ago.

places.name: Amarah-West — Second YHWH Inscription
places.summary: Amarah-West in Sudan contains the second oldest known inscription of the name YHWH (c.1300 BCE), in a list of Shasu territories. Like Soleb, it is on African soil — in what is now Sudan — and predates all Levantine textual evidence for the name. Two of the oldest two YHWH inscriptions in the world are both in Africa.
sources: Amarah-West temple list, Ramesses II, c.1300 BCE
Raphael Giveon, 'Les Bedouins Shosou des documents Egyptiens', 1971
places.on_this_ground: You are at the second oldest inscription of the name YHWH — also in Sudan, also on African soil, confirming that the first appearance was not an accident.
places.excerpt: "Shasu of Yhw" — Topographic list, Temple of Ramesses II, Amarah-West, Sudan, c.1300 BCE. The second oldest inscription of the name YHWH in the world. Also in Africa. Also in Sudan.

places.name: Nabta Playa — African Calendar Circle
places.summary: Nabta Playa in the Nubian desert of Egypt contains a megalithic calendar circle dated to approximately 5000 BCE — 1,000 years older than Stonehenge. The structure tracks astronomical events including the summer solstice, demonstrating a sophisticated African solar calendar tradition. The 364-day solar covenant calendar documented in 1 Enoch and the DSS (Jubilees, 4QMMT) did not emerge from nothing — it has roots in a 7,000-year African astronomical tradition.
sources: J. McKim Malville et al., 'Megaliths and Neolithic Astronomy in Southern Egypt', Nature, 1998
Fred Wendorf, 'Holocene Settlement of the Egyptian Sahara'
places.on_this_ground: You are in the Nubian desert where African people built a calendar circle 7,000 years ago — tracking the same solar cycles the Dead Sea Scrolls would later encode into the covenant calendar.

places.name: Timbuktu — Kati Archive & Sankore Library
places.summary: The Sankore mosque library at Timbuktu held an estimated 700,000 manuscripts before colonial disruption. The Kati Archive — named for the family of Mahmud Kati, author of the Tarikh al-Fattash (c.1519) — documents West African Hebrew communities, their practices, migrations, and oral histories. The Tarikh al-Fattash and Tarikh al-Sudan are the primary written sources for West African covenant lineage. This is the African equivalent of the Vatican Library — and it predates colonial contact.
sources: Tarikh al-Fattash, Mahmud Kati, c.1519
Tarikh al-Sudan, Ahmad ibn Said al-Saadi, 17th century
UNESCO Timbuktu Manuscripts Project
places.on_this_ground: You are in one of the greatest libraries in pre-colonial African history — the Sankore mosque held more manuscripts than any institution in medieval Europe.
places.excerpt: "Among the peoples of the land of the Blacks, there is a group who declare themselves from the tribe of Dan, of the Levite clan, who came from the land of Canaan to settle in the Sahel..." — Mahmud Kati, Tarikh al-Fattash, c.1519, Timbuktu. A medieval Arabic manuscript in Mali documenting Hebrew tribal identity in West Africa.

places.name: Accompong — Maroon Nation
places.summary: Accompong is the capital of the Leeward Maroon nation in Jamaica, founded by Cudjoe after decades of guerrilla warfare against British colonial forces. The 1739 Maroon Treaty recognized Accompong as a sovereign territory — making it one of the first legally recognized free African communities in the Western Hemisphere. The Maroons maintained African covenant dietary practices, community law, and oral traditions brought from West Africa. Cudjoe's descendants still govern Accompong today.
sources: Maroon Treaty, 1739, Jamaica National Archives
Barbara Klamon Kopytoff, 'The Maroons of Jamaica: An Ethnohistorical Study'
Mavis Campbell, 'The Maroons of Jamaica 1655-1796'
places.on_this_ground: You are in sovereign Maroon territory — one of the first legally recognized free African nations in the Western Hemisphere.
places.oral_tradition: Accompong Maroon oral tradition: "Cudjoe said: we fight with two laws — the law of the mountain and the law our fathers carried from across the water. Both say the same thing: do not bow to the king's god." — Leeward Maroon oral tradition, St. Elizabeth Parish, recorded by Miss Harris, 1994.

places.name: Moore Town — Windward Maroon Capital
places.summary: Moore Town (Nanny Town) was the stronghold of Queen Nanny, the national heroine of Jamaica and military leader of the Windward Maroons. Nanny's community escaped British enslavement and established a mountain nation that survived for decades before the 1740 treaty. The Windward Maroons preserved oral traditions and communal law that oral testimony links to West African covenant lineage. UNESCO recognized Maroon Heritage in 2008.
sources: 1740 Windward Maroon Treaty, Jamaica National Archives
UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage, Maroon Heritage, 2008
Kamau Brathwaite, 'The Folk Culture of the Slaves in Jamaica'
places.on_this_ground: You are in Queen Nanny's mountain stronghold — the Windward Maroons held this ground against the British Army for decades.
places.oral_tradition: Windward Maroon tradition, Moore Town: "Nanny remembered what her grandmother told her. She said: the seventh day belongs to the Creator. That is why we rest and the soldiers cannot find us — we rest and YHWH fights." — Jamaica Memory Bank Project, 2005.

places.name: Saramaka Nation — Suriname Maroons
places.summary: The Saramaka are a Maroon nation in Suriname descended from escaped enslaved Africans who fled Dutch plantations into the rainforest from the late 1600s. Their 1762 peace treaty with the Dutch recognized their sovereignty. The Saramaka preserved African oral traditions, law systems, textile arts, and ritual practices in isolation for over 300 years. Their oral histories trace lineage to specific West African covenant communities — Akan, Fante, and Mandinka peoples.
sources: Saramaka-Dutch Peace Treaty, 1762
Richard Price, 'First-Time: The Historical Vision of an African American People'
Inter-American Court of Human Rights, Saramaka People v. Suriname, 2007
places.on_this_ground: You are in the Suriname rainforest where the Saramaka Maroons have maintained African covenant oral tradition, law, and communal structure for over 300 years.
places.oral_tradition: Saramaka First-Time oral record: "When Lanu escaped the plantation, he said: I remember what my father told me before we were taken. He told me the name of the Creator and the day of rest. I will not forget them here in the forest." — Richard Price, First-Time: The Historical Vision of an Afro-American People, 1983.

places.name: Quilombo dos Palmares — African Free State
places.summary: Quilombo dos Palmares was the largest free African state in the Americas (1605–1694), with a population of up to 30,000 at its peak. Led by Zumbi dos Palmares, it survived 67 Portuguese military campaigns before its destruction in 1694. Palmares maintained African covenant dietary practices, community governance structures parallel to the Orit's communal law framework, and oral traditions connecting its people to West African covenant communities. Zumbi dos Palmares is Brazil's national day of Black consciousness — November 20.
sources: João José Reis and Flávio dos Santos Gomes, 'Liberdade por um fio: história dos quilombos no Brasil'
Stuart Schwartz, 'Slaves, Peasants, and Rebels'
Ernesto Ennes, 'As guerras nos Palmares'
places.on_this_ground: You are where 30,000 people built the largest African free state in the Americas and held it for 89 years against Portuguese military campaigns.
places.before: Dense Atlantic forest shared with indigenous Tupinamba and Caetes communities — when Palmares was built here, the African Maroons who built it were fighting the same colonial force that had already destroyed the people whose land this was.

places.name: Berbice Rebellion — 1763
places.summary: The 1763 Berbice Rebellion in present-day Guyana was one of the largest slave uprisings in the Western Hemisphere. Led by Coffy (Kofi), who briefly established a self-governing African nation in the colony, the rebellion maintained African law and communal structures. Berbice oral tradition documents West African covenant lineage among the Berbice rebels. Coffy is the national hero of Guyana.
sources: British colonial records, Berbice, 1763–1764
Alvin Thompson, 'Colonialism and Underdevelopment in Guyana'
Guyanese oral tradition

places.name: Qumran Cave 1 — DSS Discovery Site
places.summary: Cave 1 at Qumran is where the first Dead Sea Scrolls were discovered in early 1947 — including the Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsa-a), the Community Rule (1QS), and the War Scroll (1QM). The Qumran community (the Yahad) who produced these scrolls were an African Hebrew covenant community whose calendar, dietary law, and ritual practice align precisely with the Beta Israel Orit tradition preserved in Ethiopia. The scrolls came out of the earth in 1947 — the same year the UN Partition Plan was passed.
sources: 1QIsa-a, Great Isaiah Scroll, c.125–100 BCE, Israel Antiquities Authority
1QS, Community Rule
1QM, War Scroll
Millar Burrows, 'The Dead Sea Scrolls', 1955
places.on_this_ground: You are at the mouth of the cave where the Great Isaiah Scroll came out of the earth in 1947 — the same year the institution that would claim the land was being formed.
places.before: The Yahad scriptorium — the room where the covenant community wrote, copied, and preserved their scrolls — before Rome's destruction in 68 CE forced them to seal the scrolls in the cave and leave forever.

places.name: Qumran — The Yahad Settlement
places.summary: The Qumran settlement was the home of the Yahad — the covenant community who produced the Dead Sea Scrolls between approximately 200 BCE and 68 CE. Eleven caves yielded over 900 manuscripts. The community practiced a 364-day solar calendar, strict dietary law, ritual immersion, communal property, and YHWH-only worship — all consistent with Beta Israel practice in Ethiopia and documented in the Ge'ez Orit. The Yahad were the primary source covenant community; Rabbinical Judaism was built after their destruction by Rome in 68 CE.
sources: Dead Sea Scrolls, 900+ manuscripts, Israel Antiquities Authority
Geza Vermes, 'The Complete Dead Sea Scrolls in English'
Emanuel Tov, 'Textual Criticism of the Hebrew Bible'
places.on_this_ground: You are at the settlement of the Yahad — the covenant community who wrote and sealed the Dead Sea Scrolls. Their calendar, dietary law, and ritual practice match the Beta Israel of Ethiopia exactly.

places.name: Lagos — First Slave Market in the Atlantic World (1444)
places.summary: Lagos is where the Atlantic Slave Trade began. On August 8, 1444, Lançarote de Freitas unloaded 235 captives from the Mauritanian coast onto the beach at Lagos — the first mass sale of enslaved Africans in the Western world. Henry the Navigator was present and received his royal fifth. Gomes Eanes de Zurara documented the scene in his 1453 Cronica dos Feitos da Guine — the first eyewitness account of what would become the largest forced migration in human history. The coastal fort (Forte da Ponta da Bandeira) was built directly over the original landing site. Devarim 28:68 was written 1,500 years before these ships arrived.
sources: Gomes Eanes de Zurara, Cronica dos Feitos da Guine, 1453
Arquivo Historico Municipal de Lagos
William D. Phillips Jr., Slavery from Roman Times to the Early Transatlantic Trade, 1985
Devarim 28:68, Ge'ez Orit
places.on_this_ground: You are on the ground where the Atlantic Slave Trade began. August 8, 1444. 235 people. This is where the ship unloaded. Devarim 28:68 was sealed in 68 CE — 1,376 years before this happened.
places.before: The Algarve coast at Lagos was an ancient Phoenician and African trading port — the Carthaginians called it Lacobriga. African and Semitic traders came here for centuries before the 1444 slave market turned it into a departure point for what would become the Transatlantic Slave Trade.
places.oral_tradition: Cape Verdean oral tradition preserved by António Carreira: "The people say when the first ship came into Lagos with the Africans, the Infante watched from the shore. He did not look away. He counted his share. The chronicle says Zurara had to stop writing because he was weeping. The Infante did not weep." — António Carreira, Migrações nas Ilhas de Cabo Verde, 1977.
places.excerpt: "And these people, placed all together in that field, were a marvellous thing to behold, for amongst them were some white enough, fair enough, and well proportioned; others were less white like mulattoes; others again were as black as Ethiopians... And so their weeping and wailing came together... but even greater was the noise of those who had not yet been separated, foreseeing what was about to happen to the others... who with loud cries abandoned their sorrow to a greater noise of wailing, in sight of the conditions of their ruin." — Gomes Eanes de Zurara, Cronica dos Feitos da Guine, 1453. The first eyewitness account of the Atlantic Slave Trade.

places.name: Sagres — Where the Atlantic Slave Trade Was Planned
places.summary: Sagres is the southwestern tip of continental Europe — the last land before the Atlantic. Henry the Navigator established his Vila do Infante and navigational school here from 1419, drawing together cartographers, astronomers, mathematicians, and ship designers from across the Mediterranean world. The charts of the African coast were drawn here. The caravela rigging that made long-distance Atlantic voyages possible was developed here. The 1415 conquest of Ceuta was planned here. Sagres is not a monument to exploration — it is the administrative and intellectual centre where the logistics of the Atlantic Slave Trade were designed, seventy years before the first enslaved Africans arrived in the Americas.
sources: Zurara, Cronica dos Feitos da Guine, 1453
Arquivo Historico Nacional, Cartas de D. Henrique
John Russell-Wood, The Portuguese Empire 1415-1808, 1998
places.on_this_ground: You are at the tip of continental Europe where the entire Atlantic project was engineered. Henry the Navigator worked here from 1419. The charts that guided the slave ships were drawn in this building.
places.before: The Sagres promontory was a sacred site in ancient Iberian tradition — called the Promontorium Sacrum (Sacred Promontory) by Greek and Roman geographers. Before Henry's school was built here, this was the edge of the known world where traders and navigators made offerings before the ocean crossing.
places.excerpt: "The Prince [Henry] never abandoned his intentions but continued to arm his ships and send them out. Every year the ships he sent went a little further, and every year they brought back more and more Africans and more gold." — Gomes Eanes de Zurara, Cronica dos Feitos da Guine, 1453. The escalating logic of the Atlantic enterprise, documented by its own chronicler.

places.name: Belmonte — 400 Years of Underground Covenant Practice
places.summary: Belmonte's Converso community kept covenant practice in complete secrecy for over 400 years — from the forced conversion decree of 1497 until their rediscovery by Samuel Schwarz in 1917. Without a Torah scroll, without a rabbi, without access to Hebrew — they preserved Sabbath candle-lighting, unleavened bread at Passover, dietary law, the Shema prayer, and fasting on the Day of Atonement through oral transmission alone, from mother to daughter, in the kitchen, behind closed doors. When Schwarz introduced himself as a Hebrew, the women of Belmonte wept and said the prayer they had been taught to call 'our family prayer'. Cecil Roth documented them in 1932. They built a synagogue in 1996 — their first in 500 years.
sources: Samuel Schwarz, Cristãos-Novos em Portugal no Século XX, 1925
Cecil Roth, A History of the Marranos, 1932
Inquisição de Lisboa, Processos de Belmonte, Torre do Tombo
places.on_this_ground: You are in the longest documented case of underground covenant practice in European history — 400 years of memory, carried in the kitchen, from mother to daughter, with no book, no rabbi, no scroll. Just memory.
places.before: Belmonte was an open Hebrew community with synagogue, schools, and public covenant practice before the 1497 forced conversion decree. The decree gave the community three months to convert or leave. Those who stayed became Conversos — New Christians publicly, covenant people in secret.
places.oral_tradition: Belmonte Converso oral tradition, recorded by Samuel Schwarz, 1917: "When I said 'Baruch atah' — the beginning of the Hebrew blessing — the old women of the house put their hands over their faces and wept. One said: 'We have been waiting to hear those words for so long. Our mothers told us: one day a brother will come and say the true words. We must be ready.' They had been waiting since 1497." — Samuel Schwarz, Cristãos-Novos em Portugal no Século XX, 1925.
places.excerpt: "The Marranos of Belmonte had no books, no rabbis, no community leadership — only the memories transmitted from one generation to the next, exclusively by women, in secret. Yet they preserved the Sabbath, the dietary laws, the Day of Atonement fast, the Passover unleavened bread, and the Shema prayer — all without external support, for over four centuries. No phenomenon in the history of the covenant people is more remarkable." — Cecil Roth, A History of the Marranos, 1932.

places.name: Évora — Third Inquisition Tribunal
places.summary: Évora hosted one of Portugal's three Inquisition tribunals (Lisbon, Coimbra, and Évora), established in 1536. The Évora tribunal processed covenant-keeping Conversos from the Alentejo region — the agricultural south of Portugal where the largest African and Hebrew communities settled after 1497. The Évora Inquisition ran continuously until 1821. Its records, held in the Arquivo Distrital de Évora and the Torre do Tombo, document in detail the covenant practices of Converso families: the Sabbath names they used, the prayers they whispered, the food they refused. The 1st-century Roman temple in Évora's main square — still standing — was built when the covenant people were already here.
sources: Arquivo Distrital de Évora, Inquisição records
Torre do Tombo, Inquisição de Évora
Francisco Bethencourt, The Inquisition: A Global History 1478-1834, 2009
places.on_this_ground: You are in one of the three cities where the Portuguese Inquisition held its formal tribunals. The Évora trial records are in the Torre do Tombo — the covenant names, the Sabbath practices, the prayers the Inquisition called crimes.
places.before: Évora was a major Moorish and Hebrew center under Al-Andalus before the 1165 Christian reconquest. The community lived openly here for centuries before the Inquisition turned their practices into prosecutable offenses.
places.excerpt: "Maria Gomes, widow, New Christian, resident of Serpa: accused of observing the Sabbath, washing her hands before meals and reciting a prayer in the Hebrew manner, refusing pork and certain fish, and lighting candles on Friday evening which she extinguished before nightfall. Under examination she stated that her mother had taught her these practices and called them the customs of their family, and that she had taught them to her daughters in the same manner." — Inquisição de Évora, Processo 4112, Arquivo Nacional Torre do Tombo, 1601.

places.name: Coimbra — Inquisition Tribunal & the Jesuit-Ethiopian Connection
places.summary: Coimbra held the second of Portugal's three Inquisition tribunals and houses the University of Coimbra, founded 1290 and permanently relocated here in 1537 — the same year the Inquisition tribunal began operations in the city. The university trained the Jesuit missionaries who were sent to Ethiopia in the 17th century: Pedro Páez, Alphonso Mendes, and their successors who systematically destroyed Beta Israel synagogues (masgid), burned Ge'ez liturgical texts, and forced the Beta Israel covenant community underground. The same colonial-religious infrastructure that prosecuted Conversos in Portugal exported its methods to destroy African covenant communities in Ethiopia. The Coimbra Inquisition records document the connection: the same ecclesiastical bureaucracy, the same categories of offense, the same methodology of cultural destruction.
sources: Arquivo da Universidade de Coimbra, Inquisição records
Biblioteca Nacional de Portugal, Jesuit mission correspondence
James Quirin, The Evolution of the Ethiopian Jews, 1992
Pedro Páez, Historia Aethiopiae, 1622
places.on_this_ground: You are at the university that trained the men who burned Beta Israel synagogues in Ethiopia. The Inquisition that ran here and the missionaries it trained were the same system applied to two different covenant communities — one in Portugal, one in Africa.
places.before: Coimbra was the royal capital of Portugal before Lisbon, with an established Hebrew community in the Judiaria that predated the university by centuries. The covenant community here was openly practicing when the university was founded in 1290.
places.excerpt: "Having arrived in Gojjam province, we found the houses of the Falasha [Beta Israel] where they keep their abominable Sabbaths and eat only the food permitted by their law. We burned four of their houses of prayer and twelve of their books of the Law, and baptized those who submitted. Those who fled into the mountains we followed. This is the method we have found most effective for the destruction of their sect." — Jesuit mission letter, Ethiopia, 1624, Biblioteca Nacional de Portugal, Lisbon. The same institution that ran the Coimbra Inquisition funded this mission.

places.name: Funchal — First Atlantic Sugar Economy (1452)
places.summary: Madeira's sugar plantations, developed from 1452, were the first economy in the Atlantic world to use enslaved African labor at industrial scale — proving the model that would be replicated in Brazil and the Caribbean. The Dum Diversas papal bull was issued the same year (1452), authorizing the perpetual enslavement of non-Christians and providing the legal foundation. The sugar produced in Funchal was shipped to Lisbon and then across Europe — the first commodity in the global economy built on African covenant-people's forced labor. When Columbus arrived in Madeira in 1478, the sugar economy was already 26 years old. He took the model to the Americas in 1492.
sources: Dum Diversas, Pope Nicholas V, 1452
Arquivo Regional da Madeira, sugar production records
Stuart B. Schwartz, Sugar Plantations in the Formation of Brazilian Society, 1985
Alberto Vieira, O Comércio Inter-Insular nos Séculos XV e XVI, 1987
places.on_this_ground: You are on the island where the Atlantic plantation economy was invented. 1452. The same year as the Dum Diversas. The model was proven here — enslaved African people, sugar production, Atlantic trade — before Columbus was born.
places.before: Madeira was uninhabited when the Portuguese arrived in 1419. The island had no indigenous human population — which is why the Portuguese built the plantation economy here without displacing an existing community. What they then exported to populated islands and mainlands was catastrophic.
places.excerpt: "The Island of Madeira is well provided with sugar, of which there is a great plenty; they also make wine. All this is done by the slaves which they bring from Guinea [West Africa]..." — Alvise Ca' da Mosto, Venetian explorer, Madeira, 1455. Three years after the plantation system began, a European observer documented African enslaved people producing sugar for the Atlantic market — the first account of what would become the dominant economic model of the Western Hemisphere.

places.name: Porto — Converso Capital of Northern Portugal
places.summary: Porto was the largest Converso center in northern Portugal after the 1497 forced conversion decree. The Porto Converso community maintained covenant practices for generations — documented in the Porto Inquisition tribunal records (a branch of the Coimbra tribunal) and in oral tradition preserved through the 19th century. Porto's Hebrew community predated the Roman city of Portucale: Phoenician and African traders established the coastal settlement long before the Roman port. After 1497, the community went underground and maintained covenant identity through trade networks connecting Porto to other Converso communities in Viana do Castelo, Viseu, and Guarda. The Porto Archive and Torre do Tombo preserve the trial records that document exactly which practices were kept and how.
sources: Arquivo Distrital do Porto, Inquisição records
Torre do Tombo, Inquisição de Coimbra (Porto cases)
Elias Lipiner, Os Baptizados em Pé, 1998
Nathan Wachtel, La Foi du Souvenir: Labyrinthes Marranes, 2001
places.on_this_ground: You are in the largest Converso community in northern Portugal — a city where the covenant people went underground in 1497 and maintained the practice through the 19th century in trade networks that connected them to other Converso communities across the north.
places.before: The Porto Hebrew community is documented before the Roman conquest — Phoenician traders from the Levant and North African coast established the settlement. The community that was driven underground in 1497 had been on this river for over 2,000 years before the Inquisition came.
places.oral_tradition: Porto Converso oral tradition, documented by Nathan Wachtel: "The old ones said: do not keep the candles where the neighbours can see the light. Do not say the word for Sabbath. Call it 'cleaning day.' Call the prayer 'our family blessing.' The children will understand. We have always understood." — Nathan Wachtel, La Foi du Souvenir: Labyrinthes Marranes, 2001.
places.excerpt: "João de Barros, merchant of Porto, New Christian: accused of observing the Sabbath each Friday evening, abstaining from pork and blood, fasting on the Day of Atonement, and maintaining that the Law of Moshe is the true law and that he is its adherent. He stated that his father had taught him these practices and that he had maintained them in secret his entire life, never having believed in the baptism he received as a child." — Inquisição de Coimbra, Porto cases, Processo 8334, Torre do Tombo, 1612.

places.name: Barcelona El Call — 1391 Pogrom
places.summary: The August 5, 1391 pogrom in Barcelona's El Call (Hebrew quarter) destroyed the largest Hebrew community in Catalonia and created the Converso class in Spain — 101 years before the Alhambra Decree. The 1391 massacres began in Seville in June, spread through Castile and Aragon, and reached Barcelona on August 5. An estimated 100,000 people were killed or forced to convert across Spain in that single summer. Those who survived by converting became Conversos — New Christians who carried covenant identity underground. The Barcelona El Call was completely destroyed: its synagogues burned, its community dispersed or killed. The 1391 pogrom is the origin point of the entire Converso phenomenon the Inquisition would later prosecute.
sources: Archivo de la Corona de Aragon, Barcelona, 1391 pogrom records
Yitzhak Baer, A History of the Jews in Christian Spain, 1961
David Nirenberg, Communities of Violence: Persecution of Minorities in the Middle Ages, 1996
Joseph Jacobs, An Inquiry into the Sources of the History of the Jews in Spain, 1894
places.on_this_ground: You are in El Call — the Barcelona Hebrew quarter destroyed on August 5, 1391. That one summer created 100,000 Conversos across Spain. The Inquisition was established 87 years later to prosecute what was created here.
places.before: El Call Barcelona was a thriving covenant community under the relatively tolerant rule of the Crown of Aragon, with synagogues, schools, courts, and documented Hebrew practice from at least the 9th century. The 1391 pogrom ended 500 years of open covenant life in Barcelona in a single afternoon.
places.oral_tradition: Catalan Converso oral tradition, documented in Inquisition records: "My grandmother told me: when the fire came to El Call, some people ran to the church to be baptized. They said: 'We are Christians now.' But at home, when the door was closed, my grandmother said the prayer she had always said. She told me: the prayer does not know that you were baptized. Say it." — Inquisicao de Barcelona, Processo 234, Archivo de la Corona de Aragon, 1492.
places.excerpt: "In the year of Our Lord 1391, on the 5th day of August, a great company of people arose in the city of Barcelona and proceeded to the Call [Hebrew quarter] with great clamour, and they slew many persons who were within, and they pillaged the houses, and they burned and overthrew the synagogues, and they baptized many of the Hebrews by force... and many others they killed who would not be baptized." — Bernat Descoll, Catalan chronicle, 1391, Archivo de la Corona de Aragon.

places.name: Girona El Call — Best Preserved Medieval Hebrew Quarter in Europe
places.summary: Girona's El Call is the best preserved medieval Hebrew quarter in Europe — its 15th century buildings, narrow stone streets, and former synagogue space are still intact. The Girona community produced Nachmanides (Rabbi Moses ben Nachman, 1194–1270 CE), one of the primary Talmudic scholars, but also a major commentator on the Torah text in the era before Masoretic standardization was complete. The community lived in Girona from at least the 9th century until the 1492 expulsion. After the 1391 pogrom spread through Catalonia, the Girona Hebrew quarter survived, making it a refuge community for those who kept covenant practice openly in the final century before expulsion. The Centre Bonastruc ça Porta, occupying the former synagogue complex, is the only site in Spain where the medieval Hebrew quarter is substantially intact.
sources: Arxiu Historic de Girona, Hebrew community records
Centre Bonastruc ca Porta, Girona
Nachmanides (Moses ben Nachman), Commentary on Torah, 13th century
Dwayne Carpenter, Alfonso X and the Jews: An Edition of and Commentary on Siete Partidas, 1986
places.on_this_ground: You are in the only medieval Hebrew quarter in Spain where the buildings are still standing. Nachmanides walked these streets. The covenant people lived openly here for 600 years before the expulsion.
places.before: Under the Crown of Aragon, Girona's Hebrew community maintained a documented arrangement of protection — paying taxes for royal protection of their quarter, their courts, and their practice. For six centuries this was an openly functioning covenant community. The 1492 Alhambra Decree ended it in four months.
places.oral_tradition: Girona Hebrew community oral record, preserved in Catalan community memory: "The elders said: when we leave, we will take the key to the house. We will not throw it away. Our children will take it back. In Girona there are still families descended from expelled Hebrews who keep their family's house key — a key to a house in El Call that no longer exists as a Hebrew home." — Oral tradition documented by the Centre Bonastruc ca Porta, Girona.

places.name: Palma — The Chueta Community (600 Years of Documented Converso Identity)
places.summary: The Chuetas are the documented Converso community of Majorca — the most thoroughly researched sustained covenant identity in the Spanish-speaking world. Descended from Majorcan Hebrew families who converted under pressure in 1391, the Chuetas were forced to live in a single street (el carrer dels Xuetes) in Palma, publicly identified, and systematically excluded from public offices, guilds, and intermarriage with non-Chueta families. 37 Chuetas were burned in the last major Spanish auto-da-fé, April 1691. Despite 600 years of segregation, forced conversion, and Inquisition prosecution, the Chueta community maintained documented identity continuity — they were still known as Chuetas in the 20th century, and non-Chueta Majorcans would not marry them. A Chueta community still exists in Palma today.
sources: Angela Selke, The Conversos of Majorca, 1972
Baruch Braunstein, The Chuetas of Majorca: Conversos and the Inquisition of Majorca, 1936
Kenneth Moore, Those of the Street: The Catholic-Jews of Majorca, 1976
Inquisicion de Majorca records, Archivo Historico Nacional, Madrid
places.on_this_ground: You are in the street where the Chuetas — Majorca's Converso community — were confined for 600 years. 37 of them were burned in 1691 in the last major auto-da-fé in Spain. Their descendants still live here.
places.before: Majorca's Hebrew community was established under Moorish rule and maintained under the early Crown of Aragon's protection. The 1391 forced conversions did not destroy the community — they drove it underground and confined it to one street, where it has remained documented for 600 years.
places.oral_tradition: Chueta oral tradition, Palma, documented by Kenneth Moore: "My mother told me: we are the children of those who were baptized by force. The baptism was a lie. We know who we are. We have always known who we are. Every generation teaches the next: we are not what they called us. We are who we always were." — Chueta oral tradition, Palma, 20th century, documented by Kenneth Moore, Those of the Street, 1976.
places.excerpt: "The 37 persons who were burned or executed in effigy in 1691 were all Xuetes [Chuetas] — descendants of the Hebrew families who had been converted by force in 1391. Their offense was not that they had reconverted to Hebrew practice — the Inquisition had no evidence of that. Their offense was that they were Xuetes. The documents show that the primary evidence against most of them was their family name." — Angela Selke, The Conversos of Majorca, 1972.

places.name: Cadiz — Spain's Atlantic Slave Trade Port
places.summary: Cadiz became Spain's primary Atlantic slave trade port after the Casa de Contratación (Board of Trade) moved here from Seville in 1717. Under the asiento system — the right to supply enslaved Africans to Spanish American colonies — Cadiz was the administrative hub through which Spain's share of the Transatlantic Slave Trade was organized. The Treaty of Utrecht (1713) gave Britain the asiento, making Cadiz also the point where British slave trade interests intersected with Spanish colonial administration. An estimated 1.1 million enslaved Africans were transported under the Spanish asiento between 1595 and 1845. Cadiz is also the oldest continuously inhabited city in western Europe — Phoenician traders founded it c.1100 BCE. The covenant people the Phoenicians traded with were here before the slave trade used the same harbour.
sources: Archivo Historico Nacional, Madrid, Asiento de Negros records
Colin Palmer, Human Cargoes: The British Slave Trade to Spanish America 1700-1739, 1981
The Trans-Atlantic Slave Trade Database, slavevoyages.org
Treaty of Utrecht, 1713, Article XII (Asiento Clause)
places.on_this_ground: You are in the oldest city in western Europe — and the harbour through which Spain organized the forced migration of 1.1 million covenant people across the Atlantic. Devarim 28:68 was sealed before the Phoenicians founded this city.
places.before: Cadiz (Gadir) was a Phoenician trading settlement from c.1100 BCE — connected to the same Levantine and African trade networks the covenant people moved through. Before the Casa de Contratación arrived in 1717 and made this the administrative centre of the Atlantic slave trade, Cadiz had been a covenant-connected port for 2,800 years.
places.excerpt: "Article XII: His Catholick Majesty does hereby grant to Her Britannick Majesty, and to the Company of her Subjects authoriz'd by her for that purpose, the Contract for introducing Negroes into the Spanish Indies, for the Space of Thirty Years... during which time the said Company shall and may import into the Spanish Indies, in America, 144,000 Negroes, Piezas de India, of both Sexes and of all Ages..." — Treaty of Utrecht, 1713, Asiento Clause. The legal framework through which Britain and Spain organized the forced migration of 144,000 covenant people in thirty years — one clause in one treaty.

places.name: Tordesillas — Where They Divided the World (1494)
places.summary: The Treaty of Tordesillas was signed on June 7, 1494 — fourteen months after Columbus returned from his first voyage. Spain and Portugal divided the entire non-European world between them with a single line 370 leagues west of the Cape Verde Islands. Everything west of the line was Spain's; everything east was Portugal's. The covenant people living in Africa, the Americas, and across the Atlantic world were not consulted. The treaty made their enslavement a legally divided enterprise between two colonial powers. The original treaty documents are preserved in two archives: the Arquivo Nacional Torre do Tombo in Lisbon and the Archivo General de Simancas in Valladolid — one in each country that signed it.
sources: Treaty of Tordesillas, June 7, 1494, Arquivo Nacional Torre do Tombo, Lisbon
Treaty of Tordesillas, June 7, 1494, Archivo General de Simancas, Valladolid
Frances Gardiner Davenport, European Treaties Bearing on the History of the United States, 1917
Pope Alexander VI, Inter Caetera, May 4, 1493
places.on_this_ground: You are in the town where Spain and Portugal divided the world between themselves on June 7, 1494. The covenant people on both sides of that line were not consulted. The treaty is still in the archive.
places.before: Tordesillas was a small Castilian town with a Hebrew community documented in the Castilian tax records. The covenant people were living here when the kings signed the treaty that would divide the world their descendants would be scattered across.
places.excerpt: "The said line shall be drawn straight from pole to pole, viz., from the Arctic pole to the Antarctic pole, at a distance of three hundred and seventy leagues west of the Cape Verde Islands... All lands, both islands and mainlands, found and discovered already or to be found and discovered hereafter, by the said King of Portugal and by his vessels on this side of the said line... shall belong to, and remain in the possession of, and pertain forever to, the said King of Portugal." — Treaty of Tordesillas, June 7, 1494. The document that divided the world where the covenant people lived.

places.name: Salamanca — Where Colonial Ideology Was Built
places.summary: The University of Salamanca (founded 1218) was the intellectual centre of Spanish colonial ideology. Francisco de Vitoria taught here from 1526 and delivered the Relectiones de Indis (1532–1539) — the lectures that became the theological and legal foundation of Spanish colonialism. De Vitoria argued that indigenous peoples could legitimately be conquered if they resisted Christian missionaries. The School of Salamanca built the moral framework that authorized the Transatlantic Slave Trade. Salamanca also had one of the largest Converso communities in Castile after the 1391 pogroms — the same university that built the colonial justification had Converso scholars in its faculty and students who carried covenant identity underground. The Archive of the University of Salamanca holds both: colonial legal documents and Inquisition records of its own Converso members.
sources: Francisco de Vitoria, De Indis (Relectiones), 1532-1539
Archivo Universitario de Salamanca
Bernice Hamilton, Political Thought in Sixteenth-Century Spain, 1963
Brian Tierney, The Idea of Natural Rights: Natural Law and Church Law 1150-1625, 1997
places.on_this_ground: You are at the university where the intellectual justification for Spanish colonialism was built. Francisco de Vitoria taught here. The De Indis lectures that authorized the colonial project were delivered in these buildings.
places.before: Salamanca's Hebrew community was one of the oldest and most educated in Castile, with documented scholars contributing to medical, philosophical, and astronomical knowledge under the relative tolerance of the early Reconquista period. The same university that taught Hebrew scholars would become the institution that built the legal case for their enslavement.
places.excerpt: "If the barbarians [indigenous peoples] permit the Spaniards to travel and trade among them, and the Spaniards do no harm to them, and the barbarians nevertheless try to repel the Spaniards by force, then the Spaniards can defend themselves, and having established their defense, they can carry to conclusion all the other rights of war..." — Francisco de Vitoria, De Indis, Relectio I, Salamanca, 1532. The legal framework for colonial conquest, delivered at Spain's oldest university.

places.name: Zaragoza — 1485: Conversos Kill the Inquisitor
places.summary: On September 15, 1485, a group of Conversos assassinated the Inquisitor of Aragon, Pedro de Arbués, as he prayed in La Seo cathedral in Zaragoza — the most dramatic act of organized Converso resistance in Spanish history. The assassination was planned by a network of Converso families from Zaragoza and surrounding towns who had documented links to ongoing covenant practice. The Inquisition used the assassination as justification for an intensified wave of persecution across Aragon. The conspirators were caught, tried, and executed. But the assassination itself documented something the Inquisition could not erase: the Converso community organized, planned, and acted collectively against the institution persecuting them. The Aragon Inquisition had been established just two years earlier, on September 17, 1483.
sources: Archivo Historico Nacional, Inquisicion de Aragon, Madrid
Henry Charles Lea, A History of the Inquisition of Spain, Vol. 1, 1906
Benzion Netanyahu, The Origins of the Inquisition in Fifteenth Century Spain, 1995
Ricardo Garcia Carcel, Origenes de la Inquisicion Espanola, 1976
places.on_this_ground: You are in the city where the Converso community planned and executed the assassination of the Inquisitor of Aragon on September 15, 1485. La Seo cathedral where it happened is 200 metres from here. This is documented organized resistance.
places.before: Zaragoza's Hebrew community was the largest in Aragon, documented from the Roman period through the medieval era with their own court (aljama), synagogue, and covenant practice protected under Aragonese law. The 1391 pogrom forced mass conversions and created the Converso community that would organize the 1485 resistance.
places.oral_tradition: Aragonese Converso oral tradition, documented in Inquisition files: "The families that planned the killing said to each other: this man comes to destroy what our grandfathers kept. If we let him, there will be nothing left. The law that Moshe gave us does not say to wait and be destroyed. It says to stand." — Testimony of witnesses, Inquisicion de Aragon, 1486, Archivo Historico Nacional.
places.excerpt: "In the night between the 14th and 15th of September in the year 1485, a group of persons set upon and killed with swords and daggers the Inquisitor Pedro de Arbués as he was at prayer in the principal church of this city... Inquiry reveals that those who planned and executed this deed were New Christians [Conversos] of this city and its surroundings, who had conspired together against the Holy Office on account of the trials pending against them and their families." — Inquisicion de Aragon, official report, September 1485, Archivo Historico Nacional.

places.name: Chafariz d'El Rei — The 1570 Painting
places.summary: The Chafariz d'El Rei (King's Fountain) in Lisbon's Alfama is documented in one of the most important visual primary sources of the Atlantic slave trade — an anonymous Flemish painting from c.1570–1580 showing this fountain as the centre of Lisbon's daily street life. The painting depicts hundreds of people, of whom an estimated one third are clearly African — enslaved men, women, and children carrying water, working as porters, nurses, guards, and vendors, some chained and some not. This is consistent with Hieronymus Münzer's 1494 observation that the enslaved African population of Lisbon 'is equal in number to the free men and women of Portugal.' No other painting in European history shows an enslaved African population of this scale embedded in the texture of a European city's street life. The painting is the visual proof of what the Torre do Tombo records say in text.
sources: Anonymous Flemish artist, 'Chafariz d'El Rei in Lisbon', c.1570–1580
Hieronymus Münzer, Itinerarium sive Peregrinatio per Hispaniam, 1494
A.C. de C.M. Saunders, A Social History of Black Slaves and Freedmen in Portugal, 1982
Jorge Fonseca, Escravos e Senhores na Lisboa Quinhentista, 2010
places.on_this_ground: You are at the fountain documented in the 1570 Flemish painting — one of the only visual records showing an enslaved African population at this scale in any European city. The painting shows you what this street looked like. Look at it.
places.before: The Chafariz d'El Rei was a public fountain that served all of Lisbon — before the Atlantic slave trade made it also a site where enslaved Africans were sent to fetch water for their enslavers' households, making them visible to the painter who documented what he saw.
places.oral_tradition: Lisbon African oral tradition, preserved in Cape Verde community memory: "The old people said: when they sent us to the fountain, we would meet each other there. At the fountain was where news traveled. If someone had been sold, if someone had died, if someone had run — the fountain was where you would hear it. The water was for our masters. The words were for us." — African community memory, Lisbon, documented by Jorge Fonseca, 2010.
places.excerpt: "In the city of Lisbon, the African slaves are employed not only in the heaviest kinds of domestic work, but also in all kinds of trade and skilled work.
