They are seen everywhere in the streets — carrying loads, selling in the markets, working as craftsmen, employed as doorkeepers and porters. They are in the households of the rich, in the kitchens of the monasteries, in the hospitals. They are so numerous that they are visible in every quarter of the city, at every hour." — Garcia de Resende, Miscelânea, c.1530, on enslaved Africans in Lisbon. Written when the enslaved African population of Lisbon was at its peak — estimated at 10,000 in a city of 100,000.

places.name: Setúbal — Documented Enslaved African Port Community
places.summary: Setúbal, south of Lisbon on the Sado estuary, was one of Portugal's busiest Atlantic ports and had a documented enslaved African population dating from the mid-15th century. The Arquivo Historico Municipal de Setúbal and related Torre do Tombo records document enslaved Africans working in the city's salt pans, fishing industry, and domestic households from the 1450s through the 17th century. Setúbal is also notable for its documented confraternity (irmandade) of African enslaved and free people — a formal religious brotherhood that provided community, mutual aid, and burial rites for Africans in the city. These irmandades (brotherhoods of Our Lady of the Rosary of Black Men) were established in major Portuguese cities and in the Portuguese colonial empire wherever enslaved Africans were concentrated, and represent the earliest form of documented African community self-organisation in Europe.
sources: Arquivo Historico Municipal de Setubal, enslaved population records
Torre do Tombo, Inquisição, Setubal cases
Jorge Fonseca, Os Escravos em Setubal nos Séculos XV a XVII, 1997
Didier Lahon, 'Esclavage et confréries noires au Portugal durant l'Ancien Régime', 2001
places.on_this_ground: You are in a city where enslaved Africans built a community — a formal confraternity, their own mutual aid network, their own burial rites — inside the system that enslaved them. The Irmandade de Nossa Senhora do Rosário dos Homens Pretos of Setúbal is documented from the 16th century.
places.before: Setúbal was a prosperous Portuguese fishing and salt-trading port before the Atlantic slave trade — its salt pans were among the most productive in Portugal. When the enslaved African population arrived from the 1450s, they worked those same salt pans. The land memory is there.
places.excerpt: "Item: Irmandade de Nossa Senhora do Rosário dos Homens Pretos de Setúbal. Members: 34 enslaved men, 18 enslaved women, 12 freed persons of African origin. Purpose: the burial of deceased members, the celebration of the feast of Our Lady of the Rosary, and the provision of mutual aid to members in time of sickness. Founded: circa 1544. Masters' permission required for each meeting." — Register of confraternities, Arquivo Historico Municipal de Setúbal, c.1550. Enslaved Africans in Setúbal organized their own community inside the constraints of their enslavement.

places.name: Cidade Velha — First European Colonial City in Sub-Saharan Africa
places.summary: Cidade Velha (originally Ribeira Grande de Santiago) was founded by Portugal in 1462 as the first European colonial city built in sub-Saharan Africa. It became the primary hub of the entire Portuguese Atlantic slave trade from West Africa — the point through which enslaved Africans from the Senegambia region, Guinea coast, and inland Sahel were processed before being shipped to Portugal, Madeira, São Tomé, and the Americas. The pillory stone (Pelourinho, 1520) where enslaved Africans were publicly punished still stands in the central square. The city declined in the 17th century as the slave trade shifted south to Angola, but its 200-year run as the administrative capital of the Atlantic trade left physical evidence across the island. Cidade Velha became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2009. Among the first settlers were Converso Hebrew families who came to Cape Verde to escape the Lisbon Inquisition — they built the trans-African trade networks the Portuguese exploited.
sources: UNESCO World Heritage List, Cidade Velha, 2009
A. Teixeira da Mota and P.E.H. Hair, East of Mina: Afro-European Relations on the Gold and Slave Coast 1469–1550, 1988
Linda Newson and Susie Minchin, From Capture to Sale: The Portuguese Slave Trade to Spanish South America, 2007
Arquivo Historico Nacional de Cabo Verde, Santiago
places.on_this_ground: You are standing at the Pelourinho — the pillory stone of 1520 where enslaved Africans were publicly punished. The oldest pillory in sub-Saharan Africa, still standing in the square of the first European colonial city on this continent.
places.before: The Santiago island was uninhabited when Portuguese explorers arrived in 1460. The indigenous West African populations who were enslaved and brought here — primarily from the Senegambia coast — were the first enslaved Africans to be held on the island. They built the city. The city is their labor.
places.oral_tradition: Cape Verdean kriolu oral tradition, documented in community memory: "Our grandmothers said: we are made of three things — the ocean that brought our ancestors here in chains, the land they worked, and the language they made out of everything that was taken from them. Kriolu is that language. It belongs to us. It was made here, from the mixing the slavers forced, and it became ours." — Cape Verdean community oral tradition, documented by Manuel Ferreira, A Aventura Crioula, 1985.
places.excerpt: "The island of Santiago is the principal base of the traders who deal in Guinea [West Africa]. From here ships go to all the rivers of Guinea and all the trade is managed from here... the said island has become a place of great traffic and commerce, and in it live many rich Portuguese merchants who trade in Guinea slaves and gold..." — Valentim Fernandes, Portuguese merchant and chronicler, Description of the Coast of West Africa, c.1506–1510. The first detailed account of Cidade Velha as the hub of the Atlantic slave trade.

places.name: São Tomé — First Industrial Slave Plantation Colony
places.summary: São Tomé, in the Gulf of Guinea, was the first colony in history to use enslaved African labor at full industrial plantation scale — the prototype for Brazil, the Caribbean, and every plantation system that followed. Portugal established a settlement here from 1485. By the 1530s São Tomé was the world's largest producer of sugar. By 1550, an estimated 60,000–80,000 enslaved Africans were held on the island — more enslaved people per square kilometre than anywhere else on earth. The Kongolese, Ndongo, Benin, and Igbo peoples were the primary targets. In 1493, King João II ordered approximately 2,000 children of Hebrew families — taken from their parents who had been expelled from Spain — to be transported to São Tomé, forcibly baptized, and left on the island. Most died within months. The survivors and their descendants became the 'filhos da terra' (children of the land). São Tomé is simultaneously the first modern plantation economy and the site of one of the most documented atrocities committed against the covenant people in the Iberian colonial period.
sources: Robert Garfield, A History of São Tomé Island, 1471–1655, 1992
Arlindo Manuel Caldeira, Escravos e Traficantes no Império Português, 2013
Francisco de Andrade, Crónica do Principado de São Tomé, 1651
João de Barros, Décadas da Ásia, 1552, on the Hebrew children
places.on_this_ground: You are on the island that proved the plantation model. Everything that happened in Brazil, Jamaica, and the American South was tested here first. And in 1493, Hebrew children were left here to die — taken from their parents on the docks of Lisbon and shipped to this island. Devarim 28:68.
places.before: São Tomé was uninhabited before the Portuguese arrived in 1485. The island had no indigenous human population. What was built here — the plantation system — was not adapted from anything pre-existing. It was invented here, tested on enslaved Africans, and exported to the entire Atlantic world.
places.oral_tradition: São Tomé Forro community oral tradition: "The old people said: before the Portuguese, this island was forest and sea. The Portuguese brought us here — our grandfathers came from Kongo, from the river country, from the coast. They built everything you see. And when they had built it, the masters had no more use for them. But we stayed. This island is ours because our grandfathers made it out of nothing." — Forro community oral tradition, São Tomé city, documented by Gerhard Seibert, Comrades, Clients and Cousins, 2006.
places.excerpt: "In the year 1493, the King Dom João ordered that of the children of the Jews who had been expelled from Spain and Portugal, two thousand were to be taken and transported to the island of São Tomé, there to be baptized and settled, so that the island would be populated with Christian people... Of these two thousand children, very few survived the first years on the island, which was then wild and without inhabitants, and only a small number lived to produce descendants." — João de Barros, Décadas da Ásia, 1552. The first documented account of the deportation of Hebrew covenant children to São Tomé.

places.name: Ceuta — Where the Atlantic Project Began (1415)
places.summary: Portugal's conquest of Ceuta on August 21, 1415 was the event that opened the African coast to Portuguese expansion and set in motion the Atlantic Slave Trade. King João I of Portugal, with his sons including the future Henry the Navigator, crossed the Strait of Gibraltar and seized Ceuta from the Marinid dynasty of Morocco. Ceuta was the wealthiest trading city on the North African coast — a gateway for gold, ivory, and enslaved people from sub-Saharan Africa, connected by trans-Saharan routes to Timbuktu, Ghana, and the Sahel. When Henry the Navigator saw the wealth flowing through Ceuta, he organized the expeditions down the African coast to reach its source directly. The 1415 conquest of Ceuta is the starting date of the European Atlantic colonial project. Everything that happened in the following 400 years — the slave castles, the plantations, the Middle Passage — began here.
sources: Gomes Eanes de Zurara, Cronica da Tomada de Ceuta, 1450
Peter Russell, Prince Henry 'the Navigator': A Life, 2000
John K. Thornton, Africa and Africans in the Making of the Atlantic World, 1400–1800, 1998
places.on_this_ground: You are at the first site of the European Atlantic colonial project. August 21, 1415. Henry the Navigator stood here. When he saw the gold and the people flowing through this city from sub-Saharan Africa, he organized the expeditions that became the Atlantic Slave Trade.
places.before: Ceuta (Sebta) was the wealthiest trading city on the North African coast under the Marinid dynasty — a cosmopolitan hub connecting the trans-Saharan trade networks of West Africa with the Mediterranean. The Arabic geographer al-Idrisi documented its wealth in the 12th century. Before the Portuguese conquest, it was an autonomous African city. After 1415, it was a Portuguese military base.
places.excerpt: "Among all the cities of the world, Ceuta is the most noble and the most abundant in goods... because through it pass the goods of the whole world: from the land of the Blacks of the south come gold, ivory, skins of all kinds, and people who are brought as merchandise; from the east come silks, spices, and precious stones..." — Arabic chronicler quoted by Gomes Eanes de Zurara, Cronica da Tomada de Ceuta, 1450. Henry the Navigator read this description. Then he organized the expeditions to go directly to the source.

places.name: Arguin Island — First Slave Factory (1445)
places.summary: Arguin Island, off the Mauritanian coast, was the site of the first permanent slave trading factory (feitoria) in sub-Saharan Africa, built by Portugal in 1445. The systematic Atlantic Slave Trade began here — not as a one-off raid like the 1444 Lagos auction, but as a permanent institution, a factory with infrastructure, staff, and a regular trade route. In 1441, Antão Gonçalves and Nuno Tristão brought 10 Africans back to Portugal from the Arguin coast — the first documented African captives. By 1448, an estimated 1,000 enslaved people had passed through Arguin. Pope Nicholas V's Romanus Pontifex (1455) specifically referenced the Arguin trade as the model the papacy was endorsing. The Portuguese held Arguin until 1633, when the Dutch seized it. Arguin was also the site where the Mauritanian Berber communities — connected by oral tradition to the ancient Shasu nomads named in the Soleb inscription — were first targeted by European slave traders.
sources: Romanus Pontifex, Pope Nicholas V, January 8, 1455
Gomes Eanes de Zurara, Cronica dos Feitos da Guine, 1453
T. Bentley Duncan, Atlantic Islands: Madeira, the Azores and the Cape Verdes in Seventeenth-Century Commerce and Navigation, 1972
P.E.H. Hair, 'The Arguin Trading Castle c.1445–c.1633'
places.on_this_ground: You are on the island where the systematic Atlantic Slave Trade became a permanent institution. 1445. Not a raid — a factory. The infrastructure of the trade was built here, on this island, and then replicated across the African coast for the next 400 years.
places.before: Arguin Island was a fishing ground and seasonal settlement for the Imraguen people — a fishing community of Berber and West African descent who had lived on the Mauritanian coast for centuries. The Portuguese built their slave factory over their fishing settlement. The Imraguen people are still on the Arguin coast today.
places.excerpt: "We order and decree that our beloved son, Dom Henrique, Infant of Portugal, Duke of Viseu, and all who shall obtain his written authority, shall and may sail to the provinces of Guinea and past the cape called Bojador, and trade with whomsoever they will, and by force of arms, if need be, invade, search out, capture, vanquish, and subdue... and reduce the persons of such... to perpetual slavery..." — Romanus Pontifex, Pope Nicholas V, January 8, 1455. The first formal papal authorization of the systematic slave trade from the African coast. Written about what was already happening at Arguin.

places.name: Cacheu — Portuguese Slave Trading Fort on the Guinea Coast
places.summary: Cacheu, on the Cacheu River in present-day Guinea-Bissau, was one of the oldest and most important Portuguese slave trading centers on the West African mainland — established as a trading post in the 1580s and formalized under the Companhia de Cacheu e Rios da Guiné (Cacheu Company, founded 1690). The Biafada, Papel, Balanta, and Mandinka peoples of the Cacheu River basin were primary targets of the Portuguese slave trade. The Lançados — Portuguese traders (many of them Converso Hebrews who had fled the Inquisition to live beyond its reach on the African coast) — operated from Cacheu, living with local communities, learning local languages, and acting as intermediaries. Richard Jobson traveled in this region in 1623 and documented the Marybuck communities on the Gambia River keeping Mosaic practice — communities connected to the same network the Cacheu traders served. The Cacheu trading networks extended deep into the Sahel, connecting to the covenant-keeping communities documented in the Tarikh al-Sudan.
sources: Companhia de Cacheu e Rios da Guine, founded 1690, Arquivo Historico Ultramarino
Richard Jobson, The Golden Trade, 1623
Toby Green, The Rise of the Trans-Atlantic Slave Trade in Western Africa, 1300–1589, 2012
Philip Havik, Silences and Soundbytes: The Gendered Dynamics of Trade and Brokerage in the Pre-Colonial Guinea Bissau Region, 2004
places.on_this_ground: You are at the Portuguese fort from which the Lançados — including Converso Hebrew traders who had fled the Inquisition — operated the Guinea coast slave trade. The same river Richard Jobson traveled in 1623, documenting covenant-keeping communities upstream.
places.before: The Cacheu River was the territory of the Papel, Balanta, and Biafada peoples — covenant-connected communities documented in the oral traditions of the region. The Portuguese established their fort here specifically because the river gave access inland to those communities.
places.oral_tradition: Guinea-Bissau oral tradition, Papel people: "Our grandfathers said: the traders came first. They came to trade. Then the soldiers came. Then the ships. The traders who first came — some of them were not like the soldiers. Some of them had our people's customs: they did not eat the same things. They kept a different day. We thought they were like us. Then we learned they brought the ships." — Papel oral tradition, Cacheu region, documented by Philip Havik, 2004.
places.excerpt: "The factory at Cacheu... has been the principal point from which the trade of the rivers of Guinea has been managed since the beginning of Portuguese trade on this coast. The Lançados who live among the African peoples, having left Portugal and taken African wives and learned the African languages, are the ones who direct the interior trade and bring the captives to the coast for shipment." — Official report on the Guinea trade, Arquivo Historico Ultramarino, Lisbon, c.1680.

places.name: Luanda — 5.8 Million People: The Largest Embarkation Point in History
places.summary: São Paulo de Luanda (now Luanda, Angola) was founded by Portugal in 1576 under Paulo Dias de Novais and became the single largest embarkation point for enslaved Africans in human history. The Trans-Atlantic Slave Trade Database documents approximately 5.8 million enslaved people departing from Luanda across the Atlantic — more than from any other single African port, more than from all of West Africa combined. The primary peoples targeted were the Mbundu (Kingdom of Ndongo), the Bakongo (Kingdom of Kongo), and the Ovimbundu. The Kingdom of Kongo had been an ally of Portugal from 1483 — then Portugal turned its military capacity against the same kingdom it had called an ally. Queen Nzinga Mbande of Ndongo/Matamba (c.1583–1663) spent her life resisting Portuguese slave raids — negotiating when she could, fighting when she must, leading military campaigns against Portuguese forces from 1624 until her death at age 80. She is one of the most documented African leaders of resistance against the Portuguese. The majority of enslaved Africans taken to Brazil departed from Luanda.
sources: Trans-Atlantic Slave Trade Database, slavevoyages.org, Luanda embarkation records
John K. Thornton, The Kingdom of Kongo, 1983
Linda Heywood and John Thornton, Central Africans, Atlantic Creoles, and the Foundation of the Americas, 1585–1660, 2007
Mariana Candido, An African Slaving Port and the Atlantic World: Benguela and Its Hinterland, 2013
places.on_this_ground: You are at the port through which 5.8 million covenant people were shipped across the Atlantic — more than from any other single point on earth. The ships that left this harbour built Brazil. Devarim 28:68 was sealed before any of those ships were built.
places.before: Luanda Bay was the territory of the Mbundu people — the Kingdom of Ndongo, whose oral tradition and political structure are documented in Portuguese colonial records. Queen Nzinga's resistance campaigns are the primary historical record of what was here before the slave port. She fought the Portuguese from 1624 to 1663 — forty years — to defend the Ndongo people from the ships.
places.oral_tradition: Mbundu oral tradition, preserved in Angola: "Nzinga said to the Portuguese governor: I am not your subject and my people are not your slaves. You will negotiate with me as you negotiate with a sovereign, or you will not negotiate at all. She made him stand while she sat on one of her women — because there was no equal chair for her in his house. She came in a sovereign's chair or not at all." — Mbundu royal oral tradition, documented in António Cavazzi de Montecúccolo, Istorica Descrizione de' Tre Regni Congo, Matamba et Angola, 1687.
places.excerpt: "The said Dona Ana [Nzinga] is a woman of great courage and great spirit, who has fought the Portuguese for thirty years and who has never submitted to any condition they have demanded of her, governing her kingdom with great wisdom and making alliances with those who resist the Portuguese, maintaining herself in the field against all who have come against her... At the age of seventy, she still conducts military campaigns in person." — António Cavazzi de Montecúccolo, Istorica Descrizione de' Tre Regni Congo, Matamba et Angola, 1687. The Portuguese Jesuit who documented Queen Nzinga — the primary written record of the most sustained African resistance against the Portuguese slave trade.

places.name: Mozambique Island — Fort São Sebastião & the East African Trade
places.summary: Mozambique Island, in the Mozambique Channel off the East African coast, was the Portuguese gateway to the Indian Ocean trade — and to the East African slave trade. Fort São Sebastião (built 1558) is the oldest surviving European building in sub-Saharan Africa. Vasco da Gama stopped here in 1498 on the first Portuguese voyage to India. By the 16th century, Mozambique Island was the administrative capital of Portuguese East Africa. The East African slave trade from here predated the Atlantic trade and ran alongside it: enslaved Makua, Yao, Zimba, and Swahili peoples were shipped to Arabia, India, Brazil, and later the French Indian Ocean islands (Réunion, Mauritius). The trade from Mozambique ran continuously from the 1500s to the 1840s — long after the Atlantic trade was nominally abolished. Mozambique Island became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1991. The contrast between the Portuguese-built Fort São Sebastião (still standing) and the destruction of the communities it was built to dominate is preserved in the archive of the Arquivo Historico de Moçambique in Maputo.
sources: UNESCO World Heritage List, Island of Mozambique, 1991
Edward Alpers, Ivory and Slaves: Changing Pattern of International Trade in East Central Africa to the Later Nineteenth Century, 1975
Malyn Newitt, A History of Mozambique, 1995
Arquivo Historico de Mocambique, Maputo
places.on_this_ground: You are on the island where the oldest European building in sub-Saharan Africa still stands — built to control the East African trade that sent people from this coast to Arabia, India, Brazil, and the Indian Ocean islands. The Fort São Sebastião was built in 1558. The community it was built to control was here long before that.
places.before: Mozambique Island (Mwaze) was a Swahili trading settlement connected to the Indian Ocean commercial network — the dhow routes linking East Africa to Arabia, India, and China. The island had its own political structure, its own merchants, its own calendar. When Vasco da Gama arrived in 1498, the Sultan of Mozambique Island sent out a delegation. The Portuguese fired on them.
places.excerpt: "On this island... there is a Moor who is the lord and who has much influence over all the other Moors of this coast... When we arrived he sent his officers to welcome us and to offer us water and wood and all that we might need, and he came himself in his boats to trade with us. But when he saw that we had not the goods he expected to receive... he became hostile and refused to speak with us further, and shot arrows at our boats, and we fired on them with bombards." — Vasco da Gama's fleet chronicle, Roteiro da Primeira Viagem de Vasco da Gama, 1498. The first Portuguese encounter with the sovereign of Mozambique Island — and the first military engagement. The pattern that followed everywhere.

routes.name: Iberian Expulsion Trail
routes.summary: The Iberian expulsion corridor — from the 1391 Spanish pogroms through the 1492 Alhambra Decree (Spain) to the 1497 forced conversion decree (Portugal). The covenant people who survived were expelled, forced to convert in secret, or carried across the Atlantic as cargo. This route connects the ancient communities they left behind to the departure points of the Transatlantic Slave Trade.

routes.name: Lisbon African Heritage Walk
routes.summary: A walking route through Lisbon's African heritage sites — from the departure points of the Transatlantic Slave Trade to the fountain documented in the 1570 Flemish painting, to the archives that preserved what was done and who was taken.

routes.name: YHWH Inscription Timeline
routes.summary: The four oldest documented sites of the name YHWH — all anchored in Africa or in African Hebrew communities. Soleb 1400 BCE → Amarah-West 1300 BCE → Elephantine 5th century BCE → Qumran 250 BCE. The name appears in Africa first.

routes.name: Devarim 28 Displacement Trail
routes.summary: The covenant people's documented displacement — from the West African coast onto the slave ships and across the Atlantic. Each stop is named in oral tradition, archive records, and primary source evidence. Devarim 28:64–68 named this before it happened.

routes.name: African Covenant Evidence Trail
routes.summary: Primary source evidence of the ancient African covenant tradition — from the 7,000-year-old Nabta Playa calendar circle to the Beta Israel of Gondar. Every stop is a primary source. Every stop is on African soil.

routes.name: Spain — Inquisition and Expulsion Trail
routes.summary: The covenant people's history across Spain — from the oldest Hebrew communities in Catalonia (Girona, 9th century) through the 1391 pogrom that created the Converso class (Barcelona), the Inquisition tribunal cities (Zaragoza, Toledo), the intellectual centre of colonial ideology (Salamanca), the treaty that divided the world (Tordesillas), to the Alhambra Decree (Granada, 1492) and the Atlantic departure point (Cadiz). Twelve stops document a 1,000-year covenant presence destroyed in one century.

routes.name: Portugal — Covenant to the Atlantic Trail
routes.summary: The full covenant story of Portugal — from the 400-year underground community of Belmonte to the first slave market in the Atlantic world at Lagos (1444), the planning centre of the entire slave trade at Sagres, the first sugar plantation economy in Funchal (1452), and the archive that preserved it all at Torre do Tombo. Twelve stops connect the covenant people's life in Portugal to the Atlantic trade that carried their descendants across the ocean.

routes.name: Portuguese Atlantic Corridor — Infrastructure of the Trade
routes.summary: The physical infrastructure of the Portuguese Atlantic Slave Trade — from the planning centre at Sagres to the first conquest at Ceuta (1415), the first slave factory at Arguin (1445), the Guinea coast at Cacheu, the first colonial city in sub-Saharan Africa at Cidade Velha, the first industrial plantation colony at São Tomé, the largest embarkation point in history at Luanda, and the East African gateway at Mozambique Island. This is the skeleton of the machine — each stop is a specific documented node in the infrastructure that moved 5+ million covenant people across the Atlantic.

genetic_corridors.name: Nile Valley Covenant Corridor
genetic_corridors.description: The ancient covenant people's documented presence along the Nile — from the Ethiopian highlands through Sudan to the Levant. Two of the oldest YHWH inscriptions on earth sit on this corridor: Soleb (1400 BCE) and Amarah-West (1300 BCE). The Elephantine colony maintained covenant practice on the Nile for centuries.

genetic_corridors.name: West African Covenant Network
genetic_corridors.description: The documented covenant community network across the Sahel and West African coast — connected by the Tarikh al-Sudan, Tarikh al-Fattash, Jobson's 1623 Gambia River account, and E1b1a population genetics. E1b1a (E-M2) is the dominant lineage in West Africa and the African American population — and is the primary lineage of the ancient covenant people documented in this network.

genetic_corridors.name: Horn of Africa — Red Sea Corridor
genetic_corridors.description: The ancient coastal migration corridor from the Horn of Africa along the Red Sea — documented in 1 Enoch and Beta Israel oral tradition as the ancestral path. Population genetics (E1b1b / E-M78) traces presence along this corridor from the Ethiopian highlands through the Sinai and into the Levant.
